title: Nouns: gender and number

objectives.can: Give the gender and number of an Aramaic noun.
Recognise ten of the commonest nouns of Biblical Aramaic.

explanation.summary: Aramaic nouns are masculine or feminine, and singular or plural; a few are dual. The ending of a noun is a good clue to its gender and number, but gender is a fact about the word, and a handful of endings are shared by both genders.

sections.heading: Two genders and two numbers
body: Every Aramaic noun has a gender, masculine or feminine, and a number, singular or plural. English has no grammatical gender for things; Aramaic does. The word for 'king' is masculine and the word for 'word' or 'thing' is feminine, and the adjectives and verbs that go with them agree. Lesson A1.1.3 and the verb lessons show how.

A few nouns in the library are labelled 'common': the texts use them with both genders, or give too little evidence to decide, as with the word for 'fire' in Daniel 3. This course tests only masculine and feminine nouns, and treats the 'common' label as a note that the gender is not settled.

This lesson looks at nouns in their absolute state, the plain form without the determined ending or a possessive. The three states are the subject of lesson A1.1.2. To keep the endings in view, the paradigm tables below also show the other two states, without explaining them yet.

sections.heading: The usual endings
body: A masculine singular noun usually has no ending: the word for 'king' (in Daniel 2:10) is an example. A masculine plural usually ends in -ִין: the word for 'kings' in Daniel 2:21 is an example. A few masculine plurals are written -ִים, as in Ezra 4:13 and Daniel 4:14. Hebrew regularly uses -ים for the masculine plural; Aramaic writes -ין in nearly all of its.

A feminine singular noun often ends in -ָה, as the word for 'word' in Daniel 2:10 does. Other feminine singulars end in -ָא, as the noun for 'counsel' in Daniel 2:14, or in -וּ, as the noun for 'kingdom' in Daniel 2:39, or have no ending at all, like the word for 'stone' in Daniel 2:34. A feminine plural ends in -ָן, as the plural of 'gift' in Daniel 2:6, or in -ִין, as the plural of 'word' in Daniel 7:1. The plural ending -ִין therefore does not tell you the gender: you need the word itself.
The table summarises the usual absolute-state endings. It lists tendencies. The texts are small, and some forms a grammar lists never occur.

sections.heading: When the ending does not tell you
body: Some feminine nouns have no ending, and the only way to know their gender is to learn the word. The noun for 'stone' in Daniel 2:34 and the noun for 'hand' in Daniel 5:5 are feminine without any feminine ending. The noun for 'earth' is also feminine, though its determined form ends in -ָא like many masculine ones.

The gender of a noun is what the agreeing words show. When you meet a noun, check the adjective or verb that goes with it. In Daniel 7:3, the beasts are feminine plural, and so is the adjective 'great' that follows them.
Learn each new noun with its gender, as you would learn it with its meaning.

sections.heading: Dual nouns
body: A few nouns have a dual form, ending in -ַיִן. The library marks six occurrences of five such nouns in the Aramaic texts: 'hands' (twice, in Daniel 2:34 and 2:45), 'face' in Daniel 3:19, and 'feet', 'teeth' and 'horns' in Daniel 7. The dual is used for things that come in pairs, but it is not always used for two. In Daniel 7:7 the beast has 'ten horns' in the dual form. Treat the dual as a rare form to recognise when you meet it. Most nouns that come in pairs have an ordinary plural.

sections.heading: Reading a noun
body: To read a noun, start with its ending, then check the headword and the sense. The ending suggests the gender and the number; the headword confirms the gender; the verb or adjective that agrees with the noun is the final witness. Read Daniel 2:4 to 6 again with this in mind. You have met some of its words in lesson A0.1.2.

misunderstandings: The plural ending -ִין is not a masculine ending. Many feminine plurals also end in -ִין, such as the plural of 'word'.
A feminine noun does not always end in -ָה or -ת. The nouns for 'stone' and 'hand' are feminine with no ending.
Grammatical gender is not sex. A masculine noun need not name a male being, and a feminine noun need not name a female one.
Aramaic does not use the Hebrew plural -ים as a rule. A few forms in -ִים exist, but the usual ending is -ִין.

deeper.heading: Why the numbers are not simple
body: Aramaic nouns often show their number by more than the ending: the stem may change (a vowel disappears or a doubled consonant appears) and the plural of some nouns is formed on a different stem altogether. The word for 'king' changes its vowels in the plural, and the word for 'houses' in Daniel 2:5 has a different stem from the singular. Lessons A1.1.2 and A1.1.3 show more. Do not expect to build a plural from a singular by rule: learn the plural when you learn the noun.
